revision.text:
Regarding the website hash, Is anyone able to tell which hash function was used, or atleast which hash functions could possibly have been used. If we know this we could attempt a bruteforce attack.
-Cromwell

well, I realize brute forcing is a lengthy process, but we do know a few things. First, the last part of the string will be ".onion", Second there will most likely be 16 characters preceding that. Third, These 16 characters will most likely be lowercase a-z 0-9. This is the pattern that every other onion has followed. Maybe we could use this info to our advantage to cut down on brute force time?

What I was more leaning towards with my previous comment was if we could use this information to reduce the number of strings the bruteforce program would need to check against the hash. Because we know the most probably string length to be 21 characters long, 5 of those characters are onion and, the dataset for the other 16 charactr is composed of 36 possible characters. meaning that we have only 16^36(2.2300745198531e+43) possible combinations which I know seems daunting, but when compared to the number we'd have without these limiting factors, it is a lot less. I think what we need to do is get the community to come together and share computational power so that we can get this cracked asap.

revision.text: Possible hash types include: Whirlpool, Blake2b, Blake-512, MD6, SWIFFT and SHA-512. Most probable ones are Whirlpool (most likely this one) and SHA-512. If these fail, MD6 is the next best guess, then everything else. Brute forcing will be hard without a coordinated effort and a powerful setup. Even with hundreds of commercially available graphic cards, bruteforcing would take months. Or at least that's what I heard.
